verses.translation_literal: Ring out, [you] righteous ones, in YHWH! For the upright, praise is fitting.
verses.translation_dramatic: Ring out, you righteous! Let your voices rise like bells in the clear air, and let YHWH be the ground of your joy. For the upright, praise is no burden. It is what suits them, the way a garment suits the one it was cut for.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a summons, and the actors should play it as one: a leader calls to a gathered crowd at the sanctuary, and the crowd answers. The Hebrew verb is רנן, a vocal, high-pitched ringing cry, the sound of a festival crowd, not of a quiet hymn-sing. The KJV's 'Rejoice' keeps the joy but loses the noise. The same opening echoes Psalm 32:11 (the previous psalm ends on 'shout for joy, all you upright of heart'), and Psalm 33 has no title of its own, so the two read as a pair.

The righteous (צדיקים) and the upright (ישרים) are the covenant community, those whose conduct and heart agree with God's standard. The KJV's 'comely' is archaic: נָאוָה means 'fitting, becoming, seemly', as in Song 1:10 'your cheeks are lovely'. Praise is what suits such people, not a duty laid on them. Radak reads the line as: it is good and beautiful for the righteous to praise, for they are the ones who understand God's works.

philological_notes.note: A piel imperative, 'ring out, give a ringing cry'. Ibn Ezra glosses it simply as 'make the voice heard' (השמיעו קול). The sound is the point: this is vocal, public praise.
'Fitting, becoming'. Ibn Ezra and Radak discuss the root (a nifal of אוה, or a by-form of נאה); either way the sense is 'seemly, beautiful', and Metzudat Zion glosses it 'pleasant and lovely'.

verses.translation_literal: Give thanks to YHWH with lyre, with harp [of] ten; make music to him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Thank the LORD with the lyre; let your fingers find the strings. Bring out the harp of ten strings and play for him, not for the room, but for him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse gives two commands built on two different roots. הוֹדוּ (from ydh) means to give thanks, to confess openly what someone has done; זַמְּרוּ (from zmr) means to make music, to play and sing. They sit on either side of the instruments, so thanks and music are one act. The KJV's 'Praise the Lord' and 'sing' flatten this: the first verb is public acknowledgment, and the second is not only singing, since the instruments are its object.

The kinnor is a hand-held lyre, light enough to carry in procession; the ancient kinnor was a lyre, not the upright, plucked-strings 'harp' of later Europe, and the KJV's 'harp' for it misleads. The nevel is a larger, standing lyre or harp, and the KJV's 'psaltery' is a Greek-derived word borrowed from the Septuagint, not a Hebrew term. Actors should picture a courtyard band: small lyre in the hand, bigger harp on the ground.

עָשׂוֹר, 'ten', is the knot of the verse. Ibn Ezra reports that a Rabbi Moshe took it as a nevel with ten holes, and rejects this: the nevel is an instrument by itself, and 'ten' is a second thing, as in Ps 92:4, 'on the ten and on the harp'. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion read the same way, supplying a missing 'and' (like 'sun, moon' in Hab 3:11), with 'ten' an instrument of ten strings. Targum reads 'a harp of ten strings', which is the KJV's 'instrument of ten strings'. Perform it as the large harp with ten strings; the number marks fullness, a full instrument for a full-voiced praise.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil imperative of ydh: to give thanks, to acknowledge publicly. The sense is open declaration, more than the soft 'praise' of English; it is a verb of speech before it is a verb of feeling.

Either 'with a ten-stringed harp' or 'with harp and ten[-stringed instrument]'. Ibn Ezra rejects the view of a Rabbi Moshe that it is a nevel with ten holes, and reads two instruments, comparing עֲלֵי עָשׂוֹר וַעֲלֵי נָבֶל in Ps 92:4. Radak and Meiri read 'a missing waw'.
Piel imperative of zmr: to make music, to play an instrument with or without voice. The root gives mizmor, the heading of many psalms.

verses.translation_literal: Sing to him a song, a new one; do well [to] play with a shout of joy.
verses.translation_dramatic: Sing to him a song that has never been sung, a new one. Play it well, and let it break out into a shout.
verses.directors_commentary:
The leader keeps adding commands, each one more demanding: sing, and sing something new, and play well, and then let it burst into a shout. Play the build.

A 'new song' (שיר חדש) is a recurring psalm phrase for a song that answers a new act of God. Meiri says it means one added to the daily songs, for each miracle He does; Malbim has it renewed with each new act of providence. Radak: renew a song for Him continually. Do not play 'new' as 'modern'. The word is about fresh occasion, not fashion.

הֵיטִיבוּ נַגֵּן is an idiom of two verbs: 'do well, play', so 'play skilfully' (KJV, ASV) is right, but the Hebrew has the plain verb 'do well' as a separate beat. The weak spot in the KJV is 'a loud noise': תְּרוּעָה is the shout of a crowd, the blast of the horn at a festival or before battle (Num 10:5–6), a joyful, even royal sound. 'Noise' has lost that.

philological_notes.note: A new song, i.e. one fitted to a new act of God. Meiri: in addition to the usual daily songs, a fresh one for each new miracle; Radak: renew it always.

A shout of joy or a blast, the sound of an assembly acclaiming a king or a horn call. Meiri takes it as a sound of acclamation or a musical term; Malbim hears in it the announcement of something new and of God appearing to judge.

verses.translation_literal: For upright [is] the word of YHWH, and all his work [is] in faithfulness.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the word of the LORD is straight and true, and everything he does, he does in faithfulness.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the psalm turns from summons to reason: 'for' (כי) tells us why to sing. The reasons are God's word and God's work, and the poet sets them side by side: what He says, what He does.

'Upright' (ישר) is the same word that named the upright in verse 1, so the song fits those who are like the God they praise: straight. The KJV's 'right' and 'done in truth' soften two things. 'Is right' hides the repeated root ישר; and 'in truth' for באמונה misses the word's weight. אמונה is steadiness, reliability, something you can lean on (the root is the one that gives 'amen'). It is not a statement-truth but trustworthiness, so 'faithfulness' (ASV) is better. Note too that the Hebrew has no verb: 'upright is the word... in faithfulness all his work'.

Ibn Ezra and Radak take it as a statement of God's justice in His decrees (Radak cites Deut 32:4, 'a God of faithfulness and without injustice'); Malbim reads it as the natural order: the word that made the world is built on fixed, reliable laws.

philological_notes.note: Straight, level, upright. The same root as the 'upright' of verse 1 and Malbim's 'straight mind'. A word of line, not just of morals.

In faithfulness, with steadiness. The root of 'amen' and of 'firm, supporting'. Malbim: the fixed natural laws are called emunah because they are reliable and kept. Radak ties it to Deut 32:4, 'God of emunah'.

verses.translation_literal: Loving righteousness and justice; [with] the covenant loyalty of YHWH the earth is full.
verses.translation_dramatic: He loves righteousness and justice. And the earth, from edge to edge, is full of the LORD's steadfast love.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two lines, and two weights. First the character: God is a lover of what is right, a participle with no 'he' in the Hebrew, as if the poet cannot wait for a subject. Then the world: it is full of חסד. Say 'full' with a wide gesture.

צדקה and משפט are a pair, 'righteousness and justice', the royal ideals of the ancient Near East: the king's duty to put things right and to decide cases fairly. Applying them to YHWH makes Him the real king. The KJV's 'judgment' for משפט is old English for 'justice', and 'goodness of the Lord' for חסד is too weak. חסד is covenant loyalty, the faithful love that binds a party to a promise; the KJV translates it 'mercy', 'kindness' or 'goodness' elsewhere, so the same word does not appear twice for the reader. 'The earth is full' is a bold claim in a world where every land had its own gods and its own seasons of drought.

Radak: God does both righteousness and judgment, but חסד is the stronger force, which is why the verse ends on it (he cites Jeremiah 9:23). Ibn Ezra reads 'righteousness' (צדקה) as plain 'right' (צדק).

philological_notes.note: 'Righteousness and justice', the standard pair for just rule. Ibn Ezra takes צדקה as צדק, 'what is right', balancing משפט, and חסד as the whole that includes them. Radak links the pair to Jeremiah 9:23.

Covenant loyalty, steadfast love. It is a duty of faith between partners, more than 'goodness' (KJV). Radak: it is the quality that prevails over justice in God's rule; Metzudat David: 'He does chesed with all creatures'.

verses.translation_literal: By the word of YHWH the heavens were made, and by the breath of his mouth, all their host.
verses.translation_dramatic: By the word of the LORD the heavens were made. By the breath of his mouth, every star in their ranks.
verses.directors_commentary:
From the earth to the sky, and from what God does to how He does it. This is the psalm's creation hymn, and its claim is quiet and enormous: the heavens needed no struggle. In neighbouring cultures the sky was a god, or a body torn from a defeated god (as in the Babylonian Enuma Elish), and the sun, moon and stars were gods who ruled. Here the whole 'host' (צבא) of heaven, the word for an army and for the stars in their ranks, is the product of a spoken word and a breath.

The KJV's 'by the breath of his mouth' keeps the image, but the Hebrew word for 'breath' is רוח, the same word as 'wind' and 'spirit': God exhales, and the heavens come to be. The two parts of the line are parallel (word // breath, heavens // their host), and Radak notes that the second repeats the first. The echo of Genesis 1 ('God said') is deliberate; Radak ties it directly to the 'and God said' of the creation account. Metzudat David reads the 'host' as the angels and the spheres, a later reading the actors need not play.

philological_notes.note: 'The breath of his mouth': רוח is breath, wind and spirit at once. Radak calls the line a doubling of 'the word'; Malbim takes the breath as lighter than the word and so fitting for the luminaries.
'Their host', the stars and powers of the sky, like an army drawn up in ranks. Metzudat David takes it as the angels and the spheres; Malbim as the stars and lights hung on the fourth day.

verses.translation_literal: Gathering, like a heap, the waters of the sea; putting the deeps in storehouses.
verses.translation_dramatic: He gathers the waters of the sea and piles them up as in a heap. He lays the deeps away in storehouses, locked and kept.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the sea, the great threat. In the ancient Near East the sea and the deep were chaos itself: the Babylonian Tiamat, the Ugaritic Yam, a god to be fought. Here the sea is a heap of water, gathered by hand, and the primal deeps (תהומות) are goods in a warehouse. Play the line as a quiet shock: the monster is stock, stacked and stored.

The KJV 'as an heap' is correct: נֵד is a mound, a standing pile, and the word elsewhere describes the waters of the Red Sea standing 'like a heap' (Exodus 15:8) and of the Jordan (Joshua 3:13). Rashi and Radak read it just so, and Rashi warns that נֵד is not נֹאד, 'wineskin'. Some ancient translators read the latter, 'as in a skin bottle', an image of the sea bottled up; the Masoretic text says heap. The KJV's 'the depth' is singular, but the Hebrew has the plural 'deeps'. The participles (gathering, putting) are present and continuous, an ongoing act, not a single event in the past.

The 'storehouses' (אוצרות) are the places where kings kept grain, oil and treasure. Rashi puts them 'under the earth'.

philological_notes.note: 'Like a heap', a standing mound of water. Rashi: a word of height, as the Targum Onkelos renders Ex 15:8 'they stood like a wall'; he distinguishes נֵד from נֹאד 'wineskin'.
'Storehouses of the deeps': the deeps are stored away like treasure. Rashi: under the earth. Metzudat David: He shut them in so that they would not go out and flood the earth.

verses.translation_literal: Let all the earth fear from YHWH; from him let all the inhabitants of the world dread.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let all the earth fear the LORD. Let everyone who lives in the world tremble before him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The conclusion of the creation hymn, and the first command addressed beyond Israel: not just the righteous of verse 1 but 'all the earth'. The two lines use two different verbs of fear, ירא ('fear, revere') and גור ('dread, shrink back'), and the actors should hear the second one as sharper. Malbim says it is the greater, the fear of reward and punishment.

The KJV's 'stand in awe of him' is a gentle rendering of גור, and it turns a physical flinch into a pose. Likewise, 'the world' is תבל, the inhabited, cultivated earth, the human world, as opposed to ארץ, the ground as a whole. So the verse moves from land to people. Note, too, the Hebrew: 'fear from YHWH' (מיהוה), the verb taking 'from', as though the fear were a recoil away from Him.

Ibn Ezra and Radak draw the argument: since the whole world is God's work, it is only right that those who live in it should fear Him. Radak adds that this answers those who say the world has always existed.

philological_notes.note: 'Let them dread, shrink back in fear', a different verb from ירא. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'be afraid'; Malbim takes it as stronger than yirah.
The inhabited world. Malbim: the part of the earth that is settled. It is a poetic word, often in parallel with ארץ.

verses.translation_literal: For he, he spoke, and it was; he, he commanded, and it stood.
verses.translation_dramatic: For it was he who spoke, and it was. It was he who commanded, and it stood.
verses.directors_commentary:
The reason for the fear, in four short beats: spoke, was; commanded, stood. Play it almost without breath. The pronoun הוא is stressed both times, 'he, he'. It is He and no one else.

The KJV's 'it was done' adds a word the Hebrew does not have: the verb is simply 'and it was' (ויהי), the same verb that follows 'and God said' in Genesis 1. Likewise 'it stood fast' puts a gloss over 'it stood' (ויעמד): the creation took its place, like a servant who answers a call and stands ready. The BBE's 'fixed for ever' makes it a statement of permanence that the Hebrew leaves to the reader.

Radak says the verse could look back to creation or forward to what follows: no human can alter what God has spoken. Ibn Ezra says: He spoke 'by will and desire, not by a tool', so no instrument, no labour. Malbim hears in 'stood' the continued upholding of the earth against the sea.

philological_notes.note: 'And it was', the verb of Genesis 1 ('and it was so'). The creation answers the word at once.
'And it stood [forth]', took its place, held. Metzudat David: it stands so for ever. Ibn Ezra notes the tense is flexible (past or future) because God's power is the power of every doer.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH has broken the counsel of nations; he has frustrated the plans of peoples.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD breaks the counsel of the nations. He turns aside the plans of the peoples, and they come to nothing.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm now moves from creation to history, and the voice changes: from wonder to something harder. Behind it stand the ancient world's great powers, with their war councils and their alliances. Kings met in council before every campaign; the 'counsel' (עצה) was the strategy, and the 'plans' (מחשבות) were the schemes that carried it out. Malbim draws that very distinction: counsel is the goal, plans are the means.

The KJV's 'the heathen' for גוים is a loaded word. In the Hebrew it is simply 'nations', with no label of contempt. The verbs are strong: הפיר is 'to break, annul', the word of a vow or covenant cancelled (Num 30:9); הניא is 'to hold back, turn away' (Metzudat Zion ties both to Numbers 30, where a father 'restrains' his daughter's vow). So God is a magistrate who overturns a decree. The KJV's 'bringeth to nought' and 'none effect' are good, though they make a pair of idioms out of two sharp legal verbs.

The tense is perfect, and could be a general truth or a record of past events. Radak: even if all the nations agree, their counsel fails. Meiri: it may also refer to David's kingdom, kept in spite of its enemies.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of פרר, 'to break, annul, make void', used of cancelling a vow (Num 30). Metzudat Zion links it to the sense of nullification and prevention.
Counsel (the aim) and plans (the means). Malbim separates them this way; Radak calls the pair a doubling of the same idea in different words.

verses.translation_literal: The counsel of YHWH stands for ever; the plans of his heart, to a generation and a generation.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the counsel of the LORD stands for ever. The plans of his heart reach down from one generation to the next.
verses.directors_commentary:
The turn of the whole movement: against the counsel of the nations, the counsel of YHWH. The same two nouns, 'counsel' and 'plans', now belong to God, and the verb is the one used of creation in verse 9: it 'stands' (תעמד). What He commands stands; what the nations plan does not.

'The plans of his heart' (מחשבות לבו) matters. In Hebrew the heart is the seat of thought and will, not of feeling, so God has a mind and a purpose; this is speech about God in human terms (Ibn Ezra: 'by way of metaphor, against the plans of the peoples'). The KJV's 'thoughts of his heart' is literal, but 'thoughts' sounds idle where מחשבות means designs. 'To all generations' also smooths the Hebrew's repeated 'to a generation and a generation' (לדר ודר), a phrase that takes the reader down the line of the years, one by one. 'For ever' translates לעולם, 'for the age', as far as time reaches.

Metzudat David: no one can annul it, and it holds through all the days of the generations. Malbim sees in the generations the changing means by which one final purpose is reached.

philological_notes.note: 'His heart', the seat of mind and will in Hebrew. Ibn Ezra and Radak both call it a figure ('by way of a parable') set against the plans of the peoples.
'To a generation and a generation', the Hebrew idiom for every generation through time. Metzudat David: it holds through all the days of the generations.

verses.translation_literal: Happy the nation whose God [is] YHWH, the people he has chosen as an inheritance for himself.
verses.translation_dramatic: Happy is the nation whose God is the LORD. Happy the people he has chosen to be his own inheritance.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the nations and their failed schemes, one nation, and a blessing on it. The word אשרי is an exclamation: 'O the happiness of...'. It is a cry of congratulation, not a wish or a command. 'Blessed' (KJV) belongs to the other word, ברוך, which is spoken by or over someone; אשרי is declared about a person's lot. 'Happy' (BBE) is closer in force, though the ancient word means the settled happiness of one whose life is rightly ordered.

The nation is not simply a people who worship the LORD: the relation runs both ways. 'Whose God is YHWH' means they have taken Him; 'whom he has chosen' means He has taken them. Radak ties it to Deuteronomy 26:17–18, where Israel 'declared' YHWH to be their God and YHWH 'declared' Israel to be His treasured people. 'Inheritance' (נחלה) is land-language: the share of property that a family holds and passes down. God's inheritance is people, as Israel's is land. The KJV 'for his own inheritance' is right; the Hebrew has only 'to an inheritance for him'.

The two nouns, 'nation' (גוי) and 'people' (עם), are the same two words used of the failed 'nations' and 'peoples' of verse 10: the contrast is deliberate. Metzudat David notes that 'blessed' serves both lines.

philological_notes.note: 'O the happiness of'; a declaration about someone's fortunate state, in construct plural. Metzudat David: the word serves both halves of the verse ('blessed the nation... blessed the people').
'As an inheritance', a family's hereditary holding. Radak and Meiri connect the verse to Deuteronomy 26:17–18: Israel takes YHWH as God, and YHWH takes Israel as His people.

verses.translation_literal: From the heavens YHWH has looked; he has seen all the sons of the human.
verses.translation_dramatic: From the heavens the LORD looks down. Nothing is hidden from that gaze: he sees them all, every child of Adam, one human family laid open beneath the sky.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm turns here from the praise of creation to the God who watches. Play it quiet and level: no threat, only a steady, total attention. The two verbs, הִבִּיט 'looked down' and רָאָה 'saw', are near-synonyms set in a parallel couplet, and Meiri notes that the idea is doubled in different words for emphasis. Radak reads the verse against the saying in Job 22:14, 'thick clouds are a covering to him, and he does not see', the claim of those who think God too far off to notice; this line is the direct denial. Ibn Ezra adds that the heavens are named because they surround the whole earth, so no human falls outside the view.

The KJV 'looketh from heaven' flattens the plural: Hebrew שָׁמַיִם is a plural-form noun ('heavens'), the whole vault above, and the Hebrew verbs are perfects, 'has looked… has seen', stating a settled fact rather than a passing glance. 'Sons of men' is literal (בְּנֵי הָאָדָם), but it means 'humankind', women and men alike, and the article on אָדָם keeps it generic: 'the human'.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of נבט, 'to look at, regard', often a look down from above or with concern; here the perspective is from the heavens down to the earth. Paired with 'saw' in a synonymous couplet.
'Sons of the human', idiomatic for humankind as a whole; the generic article makes it inclusive, not 'men' in the male sense KJV suggests.

verses.translation_literal: From the established place of his dwelling he has gazed to all the dwellers of the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: From the fixed seat where he dwells, he gazes out, steady and searching, toward everyone who lives on the earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
A second line, a second angle on the same fact. Let the voice settle lower and slower: this is the throne room, not the sky. מָכוֹן, from the root 'to be firm, established', is the foundation or fixed site of a seat; in Israel's world it names the sanctuary where a deity's presence is anchored. Metzudat David takes it as the heavens prepared for his dwelling, and Radak says the verse restates v.13 in different words 'to strengthen belief'.

The verb changes from הִבִּיט to הִשְׁגִּיחַ, a rarer word. Rashi simply equates the two, while Metzudat Zion says it means watching 'with great scrutiny', and Radak points to Song 2:9, where the lover 'peers through the lattices'. So the KJV 'looketh upon' is correct but pale: the picture is of someone leaning at a window, looking intently. Note too the sound play: שִׁבְתּוֹ 'his dwelling' and יֹשְׁבֵי 'dwellers' share the root ישב, so the one who dwells looks at those who dwell.

philological_notes.note: A fixed, prepared place, a foundation; used of God's heavenly seat and of the temple as the place where his dwelling is established.
A rare verb of intent observation; Radak links it to the 'peering' of Song 2:9. In later Hebrew the noun 'hashgacha' became the technical term for divine providence.

verses.translation_literal: The one forming together their heart, the one understanding to all their deeds.
verses.translation_dramatic: He is the one who shaped their hearts, all of them together, and so he understands everything they do.
verses.directors_commentary:
No main verb: two participles hang in the air as titles of God, 'the Former' and 'the Discerner', and the actor should let the description do the work. The logic is the Hebrew one that Radak spells out, quoting Psalm 94:9, 'he who formed the eye, shall he not see?': whoever made the heart cannot fail to know what comes from it. יֹצֵר is the potter's word, the one who shapes clay (Gen 2:7), so the image is craft and intimate knowledge, not remote power.

The KJV 'fashioneth their hearts alike' takes יַחַד as 'in the same way', as if all hearts were identical. That is possible, but the more common sense is 'together, all at once': Rashi and Radak cite Rosh Hashanah 18a that all are 'scrutinised in one scrutiny', and Malbim argues that all hearts being formed in one act is why no new knowledge reaches God as deeds multiply. The 'heart' (לֵב) is the seat of thought and will, not of feeling alone, so 'considereth all their works' means 'discerns the thoughts behind the deeds'. A minority reading cited by Radak and Meiri takes הַיֹּצֵר as 'the treasurer' (as in Zech 11:13): he stores up all their hearts. I follow the potter reading.

philological_notes.note: 'The one who forms', a potter's word, used of God shaping humankind. Radak and Meiri record a rival reading as 'treasurer' based on Zech 11:13.
'Together, at once'; KJV 'alike' is a possible but narrower reading. The rabbinic reading is 'in one act of scrutiny' for all.
'The one who understands, discerns', literally 'attends to'; the knowledge in view is penetrating, not merely observing.

verses.translation_literal: There is not a king saved by greatness of army; a warrior is not delivered by greatness of strength.
verses.translation_dramatic: No king was ever saved by the size of his army. No warrior ever escaped by the sheer weight of his strength.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the psalm swings from the watching God to the failure of human power, and the delivery should sharpen: two blunt negatives, like two doors closing. The king and the warrior are the figures every ancient hearer trusted: in the Near East the king's salvation was his army, and the royal inscriptions boast of numbers. Radak names the cases Israel remembered: Assyria's king Sennacherib, whose vast host lay dead one morning (2 Kgs 19:35), and the giant Goliath, felled by a boy.

The repetition is the Hebrew's design: בְּרָב 'by greatness of' appears twice, בְּרָב־חַיִל and בְּרָב־כֹּחַ, and the verse is a perfect chiasm of the two nouns for force (חַיִל 'army, might', כֹּחַ 'strength'). חַיִל is both an army and its power, so KJV 'host' is right for the first and 'strength' for the second. KJV 'a mighty man' softens גִּבּוֹר, the professional warrior, the hero in the field. Malbim notes the verse moves from quantity (many troops) to quality (great strength): neither suffices.

philological_notes.note: Both 'army' and the 'might' of one; Metzudat Zion glosses it 'forces, people'. Here the army, as the king's means of rescue.
The seasoned fighter, the champion; not just 'a strong man'. Radak ties it to Goliath.

verses.translation_literal: A lie, the horse, for victory; and by the greatness of its strength it does not rescue.
verses.translation_dramatic: The war-horse is a lie when it comes to winning. For all its mighty strength, it cannot carry its rider out of danger.
verses.directors_commentary:
The third blow, and the sharpest: the horse itself is called a lie. שֶׁקֶר, 'falsehood, deceit', is the word for a broken promise; the horse promises victory and does not keep its word. Say it with scorn, not anger. In Israel's world the horse and chariot were the prestige weapons of the great powers (Egypt, Assyria), and Israel's kings were warned against building a cavalry (Deut 17:16). Radak recalls Job 39:19, where God asks, 'Do you give the horse its might?': the strength is on loan, and he can take it back.

KJV 'a vain thing for safety' blurs two points. First, שֶׁקֶר is stronger than 'vain': it is a lie, a false hope (BBE comes closest). Second, תְּשׁוּעָה is victory or deliverance, the same root as 'saved' in v.16, so the verse completes the chain. Ibn Ezra notes that the verb יְמַלֵּט ('rescue') lacks its object in the Hebrew: it means 'rescue his life', and the dramatic layer makes that a rider. The 'king' of v.16 is not named again; the horse stands for the whole apparatus of royal power.

philological_notes.note: 'Lie, deception'; the horse deceives those who trust it. KJV 'vain thing' is too mild.
'Rescues, lets slip away to safety'; the object (the rider's life) is left unstated.

verses.translation_literal: Behold, the eye of YHWH [is] toward those who fear him, toward those who wait for his steadfast love,
verses.translation_dramatic: Look. The eye of the LORD is turned, and it does not rest on the horse or the army. It rests on those who stand in awe of him, on those who wait, empty-handed and expectant, for his steadfast love.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse opens with a pointing word, hinneh, "Look!", and the singer turns the audience's eyes from the king, the army and the war-horse of the last verses to a single, unarmed object: the eye of God. Play it as a shift in gaze, not a rise in volume. Ibn Ezra reads "the eye of the LORD" as a protective look and cites two parallels that use the same idiom: Gen 44:21, "that I may set my eyes upon him" (Judah quoting Joseph's words about Benjamin), and Jer 39:12, "set your eyes on him" (Nebuchadnezzar's order about Jeremiah). In both, the eye means watchful care. That is the sense here: the eye is not surveillance but providence, a gaze that keeps watch over those it looks at.

The word "fear" (yere'av) is not terror. It is the reverent loyalty a subject owes a sovereign, and Ibn Ezra stresses that this fear is directed to God alone, not to a flesh-and-blood king. The second line gives the posture: lamyachalim, "those who wait" or "hope," from yachal, to wait with tension, like a rope pulled taut. The KJV's "hope in his mercy" is acceptable but softens two things. First, "mercy" is weaker than chesed, the covenant loyalty God has bound himself to. Second, the Hebrew has "for his chesed", with the preposition le-, so the waiting is directed toward it, with the expectation that it will arrive. The KJV also supplies "is upon" and repeats it, where the Hebrew has the bare preposition 'el, "toward." The ancient audience would hear this against the previous verses: a king's safety was measured in chariots and cavalry, and here the singer says the real guard is a gaze.

philological_notes.note: "The eye of YHWH" is a figure for watchful, protective providence. Ibn Ezra explains it by two parallels in which a person's eyes are set on another to look after them (Gen 44:21; Jer 39:12).
A participle of yachal, "to wait, to hope," which implies patient, expectant waiting rather than a vague wish. The preposition le- aims the waiting at God's chesed, as at something due to arrive.
Chesed is loyal, covenantal love, a commitment kept, and is wider than "mercy" (KJV) or "kindness" (YLT). The same word is the refrain of the whole psalm (vv. 5, 18, 22).

verses.translation_literal: To deliver from death their life, and to keep them alive in the famine.
verses.translation_dramatic: To pull their lives back from the edge of death, and in the lean season of famine, to keep them alive.
verses.directors_commentary:
The purpose clause of v.18: why the eye watches. Two rescues, one from the sword and one from hunger, are the two great dangers an ancient people faced. Ibn Ezra reads the death as 'sword or pestilence', Radak as death in battle, so the verse matches the war of vv.16–17, then adds famine, the other enemy of a village economy living on one rainfall and one harvest. The Hebrew has the definite article, 'the famine': the one every hearer feared, the failure of the rains.

KJV 'soul' for נֶפֶשׁ is misleading to a modern reader. נֶפֶשׁ is the living self, even the throat, the thing that breathes and hungers: 'deliver their life from death' is exact. The verb לְחַיּוֹתָם is the Piel of 'live', 'to give life, preserve alive', a stronger verb than 'keep': it is the same verb as the revival of the dying.

philological_notes.note: 'Their life, their very self', the whole living person; KJV 'soul' suggests a separable spirit that the Hebrew does not.
'In the famine', with the article: the dreaded famine. Radak reads it as famine coming on the whole world; Malbim as a specific famine of Israel.

verses.translation_literal: Our life has waited for YHWH; our help and our shield, he.
verses.translation_dramatic: We, our whole selves, wait for the LORD. He is our help. He is our shield.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice changes: from description to confession, from 'they' to 'we'. After the third-person lines of vv.13–19 the community steps forward and speaks. Pitch it warm, a little worn by waiting. Ibn Ezra reads it as the people saying, because we have seen the God-fearers rescued, 'our soul waits'. Malbim adds that the waiting may be long (he cites Ps 32:3, 'my bones wasted away'), and the verse says the rescue came even so.

The pronoun הוּא at the end carries the stress: 'our help and our shield, HE'. Ibn Ezra sets the pair against the king's army of v.16: 'help' answers the army, 'shield' answers the king. מָגֵן is the small round or large body shield of a soldier, and God is called a shield at Gen 15:1 and often in the Psalms. The KJV is accurate here; BBE's 'our salvation' is a mistranslation of מָגֵן. The verb חִכְּתָה, 'waited', is a rarer, more intense word than the usual 'wait' and implies holding out, expecting.

philological_notes.note: A Piel perfect meaning 'has waited, has held out in expectation'; the perfect expresses a continuing state. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'hoped'.
'Shield, protector', the soldier's defensive weapon; set against the king's army of v.16.

verses.translation_literal: For in him our heart rejoices; for in the name of his holiness we have trusted.
verses.translation_dramatic: In him our hearts find joy, because we have trusted in his holy name.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the waiting turns to gladness. Let the voice lift on 'rejoices'. The verse has two כִּי clauses, 'for… for…', that give the reason in a pair: the joy and the trust are one thing seen twice (Metzudat David: his deliverance is the joy, and he is known to save those who trust in him). Ibn Ezra relates it back to v.18, 'those who fear him'.

The 'heart' (לֵב) is the mind and will, set deliberately against the 'hearts' he formed in v.15. In the ancient world a 'name' was not a label but the person's reputation and presence: to trust 'in the name of his holiness' is to rest on who he has shown himself to be, the God whose holy name is invoked over his people (Malbim cites Jer 14:9). KJV 'shall rejoice… have trusted' turns the tenses: the verb for rejoicing is imperfect, a continuing, habitual joy, and 'we have trusted' is a completed act that grounds it. 'His holy name' is also a smoothing of 'the name of his holiness', a genitive construction that makes holiness the name's essence.

philological_notes.note: 'The name of his holiness': the divine name as the sum of his set-apart nature, in a construct chain more concrete than KJV's adjective 'holy'.
'We have trusted': secure reliance, in contrast with the hoping/waiting of vv.18–20.

verses.translation_literal: May your covenant loyalty be, YHWH, upon us, just as we have waited for you.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let your faithful love rest on us, O LORD, as surely as we have waited for you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The last line is a prayer, and the shift from statement to petition is the whole psalm's turn: after the wise watching and the failure of arms, a single wish. Say it low, almost a whisper, after the lift of v.21. The verb is jussive, יְהִי, 'let it be, may it be': this is not a claim but a request. Meiri calls it a prayer that closes the psalm, and Radak reads it as asking for the loyalty in every time.

The key is חֶסֶד again, covenant loyalty, now addressed directly to YHWH in the second person: the psalm that opened with 'rejoice' (v.1) ends with the people's own appeal. The KJV 'according as we hope in thee' is fair, but כַּאֲשֶׁר means 'just as, in proportion as': Metzudat David reads it 'as the hope, so the loyalty'. The wish is that God's loyalty will match the weight of their waiting. Malbim hears an additional plea that the waiting not be long. The verb יִחַלְנוּ repeats the root of the 'waiters' in v.18, closing the arc.

philological_notes.note: 'Just as, in proportion as'; it makes the hoped-for loyalty answer the measure of the hope.
'We have waited, hoped'; the same root as מְיַחֲלִים in v.18, closing the unit.
